paragraphs.context: Years ago, I spent several months in India
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer once lived in India for some months.
paragraphs.simple: Many years ago the writer spent a few months in India. She thought it was a very colourful and interesting country. Writing this book let her go back there in her mind.

background.note: India is a very big country in South Asia. It has many people, old temples, forests and wild animals like tigers, elephants and rhinos.

paragraphs.context: To learn more about tigers, I visited the world-famous Bronx Zoo
paragraphs.mainIdea: She went to a zoo to learn about tigers. Tigers are in danger.
paragraphs.simple: To learn about tigers, the writer went to a famous zoo in New York. She learned that tigers may disappear from the earth, because poachers kill so many of them. Good zoos teach people to protect wild animals.

background.note: The Bronx Zoo is one of the biggest zoos in the USA. It is in New York City.
New York City is the biggest city in the USA.

paragraphs.context: As I wrote this book, the plight of the tiger greatly touched my heart.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer feels sad for tigers and hopes people will save them.
paragraphs.simple: The tigers' bad situation made the writer very sad. She hopes it makes you sad too, and that people everywhere will work together fast to save tigers.
paragraphs.tone: Warm and serious. "Touched my heart" means made me feel a lot.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the story of the magic tree house began.
paragraphs.simple: One summer day a strange tree house was suddenly in the woods near Jack and Annie's town.

background.note: Frog Creek is the small town in Pennsylvania, USA, where Jack and Annie live. The magic tree house is in the Frog Creek woods.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie soon discovered that the tree house was magic.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house can take them to the places in its books.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house was magic. If they pointed to a picture in a book and made a wish, the tree house took them there.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.simple: They learned that the tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She is a magic librarian from long ago. She travels through time and collects books.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic woman in the old stories about King Arthur. In these books she is a kind librarian.
King Arthur is a king in old British stories. He lived in a castle called Camelot with his knights.

paragraphs.context: In Books #9–12, they solved four ancient riddles and became Master Librarians.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A list of their earlier adventures.
paragraphs.simple: In earlier books they saved Morgan from magic, answered four very old riddles and became Master Librarians.

background.note: In the series, Jack and Annie become "Master Librarians", people who are very good at finding things out from books.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House Books #17–20, Jack and Annie must be given four special gifts
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their new job: get four gifts to free a dog from a spell.
paragraphs.simple: In books 17 to 20 they must get four special gifts to free a dog from magic. They already have a gift from the Titanic and one from the Lakota. Now they will go to find the third gift.

background.note: The Titanic was a very big ship. It hit an iceberg and sank in 1912. Jack and Annie went there in book 17.
The Lakota are a Native American people of the Great Plains in the USA. Jack and Annie visited them in book 18.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie walked past the Frog Creek woods on their way home from the library.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie miss the little dog Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: On the way home from the library, Jack and Annie walk past the woods. They talk about how much they miss Teddy.

paragraphs.context: “He’s a really smart dog,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They list all the good things about Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: They say Teddy is clever, brave, wise and funny. Then Annie says "And here!" because she suddenly sees him.
paragraphs.tone: A fun little game: the last word "here" is a surprise.

paragraphs.context: A small dog with tan-colored fur was peeking out from the bushes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy is back.
paragraphs.simple: A small light brown dog was looking out from the bushes. It was Teddy.

paragraphs.context: She and Jack raced after Teddy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They run after Teddy into the woods.
paragraphs.simple: They ran after Teddy. The woods were bright with late afternoon sun.

paragraphs.context: The dog ran between the trees and finally stopped at a rope ladder.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy takes them to the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy ran to the rope ladder. It hung from the tallest tree and went up to the magic tree house.

paragraphs.context: Teddy waited for Jack and Annie to catch up.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy waits for them, happy.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy waited until they came to him. He breathed fast and moved his tail.

paragraphs.context: Teddy sneezed, as if to say, Of course!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy seems to answer "yes".
paragraphs.simple: Teddy sneezed. It looked like his way of saying "Of course!"

paragraphs.context: They climbed into the tree house. There was the note from Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan's note is still there.
paragraphs.simple: In the tree house they found Morgan's note on the floor, in the same place as two days before.

paragraphs.context: This little dog is under a spell and needs your help.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan's note tells them what they need.
paragraphs.simple: The note says the dog is under a magic spell. To free him, they must be given four special things.

paragraphs.context: A gift from a forest far away,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The third line of the rhyme: the gift they need now.
paragraphs.simple: This is the third gift on Morgan's list. Now they must find a gift from a faraway forest.

paragraphs.context: Jack touched the first two gifts, which they had already gotten
paragraphs.mainIdea: They have two gifts already.
paragraphs.simple: Jack touched the two gifts they already had: a pocket watch from the Titanic and an eagle feather from the Lakota.

background.note: The Great Plains are very large, flat grasslands in the middle of North America.

paragraphs.context: She and Jack looked around the tree house for one of the research books
paragraphs.mainIdea: They look for the book that will take them on the trip.
paragraphs.simple: They looked for the book Morgan always leaves them. Teddy put his foot on a book in the corner.

paragraphs.context: Jack picked it up and read the title: Wildlife of India.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book is about animals in India.
paragraphs.simple: The book was called Wildlife of India. India is very far away.

background.note: This is the made-up research book in the story. It tells about the wild animals of India.

paragraphs.context: “Let’s get going,” said Annie, “so we can free Teddy.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to go now.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they should leave now, so that they can free Teddy from the spell.

paragraphs.context: The tree house started to spin.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The magic trip starts.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house turned round and round, faster and faster. Then nothing moved.

paragraphs.context: The warm air burst with sound.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They arrive in a noisy Indian forest.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the warm air was full of loud animal sounds.

paragraphs.context: The sky was lit by an orange glow as the sun went down.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is evening, at the edge of a forest.
paragraphs.simple: The sun was going down and the sky was orange. The tree house was in a tree by a small river.

paragraphs.context: Just then, two creatures leaped onto the windowsill.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two animals jump onto the window.
paragraphs.simple: Two animals suddenly jumped onto the window shelf. Jack and Annie shouted and jumped back.

paragraphs.context: Two small monkeys peered at them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two monkeys look at them.
paragraphs.simple: Two small monkeys looked at them carefully. They had dark faces with grey fur around them, like children in warm winter coats.
paragraphs.tone: Funny picture: the monkeys look like they are wearing parkas.

paragraphs.context: “Cool,” said Annie. She turned to Jack. “Her name is Kah. His name is Ko.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie names the monkeys from their sounds.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the monkeys told her their names: Kah and Ko.

background.note: Kah and Ko are the monkeys' names. Annie takes them from the sound "Kah-ko" that the monkeys make.

paragraphs.context: “I bet he is her brother,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A joke about "Oh, brother".
paragraphs.simple: Jack says "Oh, brother!" because he thinks Annie is being silly. Annie makes a joke: maybe Ko really is Kah's brother.
paragraphs.tone: A word joke. The monkeys "laugh" at it.

paragraphs.context: Using their long tails and arms, they swung from branch to branch.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkeys climb down.
paragraphs.simple: The monkeys used their tails and arms to swing from branch to branch. Then they jumped to the ground.

paragraphs.context: This monkey is called a langur (say lun-GOOR).
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack learns what kind of monkey it is.
paragraphs.simple: The book says these monkeys are called langurs. The word means "having a long tail".

background.note: Langurs are grey monkeys with black faces and long tails. They live in India and eat leaves and flowers.

paragraphs.simple: Jack wrote a note in his notebook. (In this e-book, Jack's note is a picture, so there is no text after "He wrote:".)

paragraphs.context: Kah bounded over to Jack and grabbed his hand.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkey takes Jack's hand.
paragraphs.simple: Kah jumped over to Jack and took his hand. The monkey's hand felt like a very small human hand.

paragraphs.context: The langurs climbed the huge, leafy trees.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkeys swing through the trees.
paragraphs.simple: The monkeys climbed the big trees and swung from branch to branch, like children playing in a park.

background.note: A jungle gym is a big frame of metal bars in a playground. Children climb and swing on it.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, wait!” Jack called, hurrying after them all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants Annie to be careful.
paragraphs.simple: Jack shouts to Annie to go slower. They do not know this place.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is careful, Annie is brave. This is how they always are.

paragraphs.context: The sunset gave the trees a fiery glow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The forest is very beautiful.
paragraphs.simple: The evening sun made the trees look red and orange like fire.

paragraphs.context: Blue peacocks spread their tails.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beautiful birds open their tails.
paragraphs.simple: Blue birds with long tails opened them wide, like big fans.

background.note: The peacock is the national bird of India. The male has a long blue and green tail with "eyes" on it.

paragraphs.context: “It’s like paradise,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie loves this place.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the forest is like a perfect, beautiful place.

background.note: Paradise is a perfect place, like the garden in old stories where everyone is happy.

paragraphs.context: “ ‘Wildlife’ means scary animals, too.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says the forest also has dangerous animals.
paragraphs.simple: Jack reminds Annie that "wildlife" also means frightening animals.

paragraphs.context: Jack noticed long, deep gashes in a tree as they walked by.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees deep cuts in a tree.
paragraphs.simple: Jack saw long, deep cuts in a tree. He wanted to know what made them.

paragraphs.context: Tigers sharpen their claws on tree trunks.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A tiger made the cuts.
paragraphs.simple: The book says tigers make their nails sharp on trees. So a tiger was here not long ago.

paragraphs.context: A wild tiger eats almost 5,000 pounds of fresh raw meat a year.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tigers eat a lot of meat.
paragraphs.simple: A tiger eats about 2,250 kilos of uncooked meat in one year.

background.note: 5,000 pounds is about 2,270 kilograms.

paragraphs.context: Tigers usually leave elephants alone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tigers keep away from elephants and wild dogs.
paragraphs.simple: Tigers do not usually attack elephants. They also stay away from wild dogs.

paragraphs.context: “Wild dogs, not a shrimp like you,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack jokes that Teddy is too small to frighten a tiger.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Teddy that tigers are afraid of big wild dogs, not small dogs like him. A tiger could eat Teddy very fast.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is joking, but Teddy is not happy: he growls.

paragraphs.context: The small deer made short barking sounds and stamped their hooves.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The animals are afraid of something.
paragraphs.simple: The monkeys, birds and deer all make noises. The deer hit the ground with their feet.

paragraphs.context: This time, a deep, fierce growl answered back.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A tiger is near.
paragraphs.simple: A low, angry sound came back. It seemed to be all around them. Jack was so afraid that his hair stood up.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s hands were shaking as he put his backpack on.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They climb a tree to be safe.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's hands shook. He held a branch, pushed with his feet and pulled himself up into the tree.

paragraphs.context: The sky above was no longer glowing.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is getting dark.
paragraphs.simple: The orange sky was gone. Now it was the grey of early evening.

paragraphs.context: “How can we get through the forest without running into him?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: How can they get past the tiger?
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks how they can walk through the forest and not meet the tiger. It is getting dark, too.

paragraphs.context: Then, far below, he saw the tree trunk move!
paragraphs.mainIdea: A huge snake climbs their tree.
paragraphs.simple: Far below, the tree seemed to move. It was a snake as thick as the tree.

paragraphs.context: To kill its prey, the python squeezes it to death
paragraphs.mainIdea: How a python kills.
paragraphs.simple: A python holds an animal very tightly until it dies. Then it eats it in one piece. It can eat an animal as big as a deer.

background.note: Pythons are some of the biggest snakes in the world. The Indian python can be more than 6 metres long.

paragraphs.context: “This is more than just yuck, Annie,” said Jack. “This is life or death,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says this is very serious.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it is not only unpleasant, it is dangerous: they could die. (The book has a comma, not a full stop, at the end of what Jack says.)

paragraphs.context: The langurs swung through the air like trapeze artists.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkeys show them how to escape.
paragraphs.simple: The monkeys held long plants and swung to another tree, like people in a circus.

background.note: Trapeze artists are circus performers who swing high in the air on short bars hanging from ropes.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked back at the python.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The snake is very close.
paragraphs.simple: The snake was still going up the tree. It was almost at their branch. Jack took a big breath and held a vine.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt his stomach drop.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They swing out of the tree.
paragraphs.simple: As they swung, Jack felt like he was falling inside. Air rushed past and leaves hit him.

paragraphs.context: Like a flame, a tiger leaped up from the bushes!
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tiger jumps at them.
paragraphs.simple: An orange tiger jumped up like fire. Its eyes shone, its teeth looked like knives, and its nails almost hit them.
paragraphs.tone: Very exciting and frightening. The short sentences make it fast.

paragraphs.context: Jack threw one leg around the trunk.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They reach the other tree safely.
paragraphs.simple: Jack put his leg around the tree, let go of the vine and held a branch tightly. He was too surprised to think.

paragraphs.context: “Fun? Are you nuts?” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cannot believe Annie had fun.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says it was fun. Jack asks if she is crazy. Annie says the swinging was fun, but the tiger was frightening.

paragraphs.context: From below came loud sounds of chewing, smacking, and crunching.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Something is eating below them.
paragraphs.simple: They hear loud eating sounds. Jack thinks the tiger is eating the tree.
paragraphs.tone: A funny moment after the fear.

paragraphs.context: “Look!” Annie pointed at the twilight.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is an elephant, not a snake.
paragraphs.simple: A long grey thing moved in the air. Jack thought it was another snake, but it was an elephant's nose.

paragraphs.context: In the gray gloom, they saw a herd of elephants.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see many elephants.
paragraphs.simple: In the grey half-dark they saw a group of elephants eating leaves and grass.

paragraphs.context: “I know how to escape the tiger,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie has an idea.
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers that tigers do not attack elephants. So they can ride through the forest on an elephant's back.

paragraphs.context: She climbed down the tree until she was close to the elephant’s back.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie gets on the elephant.
paragraphs.simple: Annie climbed down, put her feet on the elephant's back, let go of the branch and sat down slowly.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry, it’s just me,” Annie said softly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie talks kindly to the elephant.
paragraphs.simple: The elephant made a low sound and moved. Annie told her not to worry, touched her back and thanked her, using the name Saba.

background.note: Saba is the name Annie gives the elephant. Annie says the elephant "told" her.

paragraphs.context: “That’s her name,” said Annie. “She just told me.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says the elephant told her its name.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the elephant is called Saba. Jack does not believe the elephant told her, so he says "Yeah, right."

paragraphs.context: He patted the elephant’s head. Her skin was rough and wrinkled.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets on the elephant too.
paragraphs.simple: Jack touched the elephant's head. Her skin was hard and had many lines.

paragraphs.context: The rest of the herd followed in line.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The elephants walk through the forest.
paragraphs.simple: All the elephants walked one after another. Saba moved slowly and smoothly, like waves on the sea.

paragraphs.context: Fireflies blinked. The moon lit a path between the trees
paragraphs.mainIdea: A beautiful night walk.
paragraphs.simple: Small insects made little lights. The moon lit a path as the elephants walked on.

paragraphs.context: The elephants paid no attention.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The elephants are not afraid.
paragraphs.simple: The elephants did not care about the growl. They walked on under the vines and through open places full of mist.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, a long roar split the night.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A long, sad sound fills the forest.
paragraphs.simple: A loud roar broke the quiet night. Then it became a long, sad cry, as if the whole forest was crying.

paragraphs.context: Jack rocked in sleepy rhythm with Saba’s walk.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack falls asleep on the elephant.
paragraphs.simple: The elephant's walk moved Jack gently. He heard Teddy sleeping, and soon he fell asleep too.

paragraphs.context: Jack slowly came out of his dream.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wakes up in the morning.
paragraphs.simple: Jack woke up suddenly. For a moment he did not know where he was. Then he remembered: he was on an elephant in India.

paragraphs.context: He sat up. Through the haze, he saw that Saba was standing on a muddy stream bank.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is morning by the stream.
paragraphs.simple: Saba was standing by the stream. The other elephants were washing each other with water.

paragraphs.context: She was sitting on a big black rock downstream.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is wet and happy.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sat on a rock. She had no shoes on and was very wet. She tells Jack to slide off the elephant into the mud.

paragraphs.context: Jack slid down her side—feet first—and fell into the mud.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets down into the mud.
paragraphs.simple: Jack slid down and fell into the mud. His hands went into the mud and his glasses got dirty.

paragraphs.context: Yellow and blue water birds spread their wings.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The morning forest is beautiful.
paragraphs.simple: Birds opened their wings, plants moved in the light wind, and big white flowers sat on the water.

paragraphs.context: Then Jack saw a strange sight.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Something strange is in the water.
paragraphs.simple: Jack saw a horn and two ears coming out of the water.

paragraphs.context: The one-horned rhinoceros, or “rhino,” washes in a forest stream.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack reads about rhinos.
paragraphs.simple: Rhinos are not usually dangerous. But they cannot see well, so sometimes they run at things by mistake. A loud noise usually stops them.

background.note: The Indian rhino has one horn on its nose. (African rhinos have two.) It lives in wet grasslands and forests in India and Nepal.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt sorry for the rhinos.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A small joke from Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks it is a pity animals cannot wear glasses, like he does.
paragraphs.tone: Jack wears glasses, so this is a funny, kind thought.

paragraphs.context: The Indian rhino is a very endangered animal.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rhinos are in danger because of poachers.
paragraphs.simple: There are very few Indian rhinos left. Bad people kill them and sell parts of their bodies as medicine and good-luck things.

background.note: Some people believe that a rhino's horn can bring luck or work as medicine. This is not true, but poachers kill rhinos to sell their horns.

paragraphs.context: The rhino rose from the stream.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rhino comes up and looks at Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The rhino came up out of the water. It looked like a very old animal from a swamp.

paragraphs.context: Annie clapped her hands and shouted, “We come in peace!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie stops the rhino with a loud noise.
paragraphs.simple: Annie made a loud noise, as the book said. The rhino stopped and went back into the water.

background.note: "We come in peace" is a famous line from old films, when visitors meet strangers and say they are friends.

paragraphs.context: “Jack!” shouted Annie. She was racing toward him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie has found something terrible.
paragraphs.simple: Annie ran to Jack with Teddy close behind her. She was almost crying.

paragraphs.context: As Jack got closer, he saw a tiger.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A tiger is caught in a trap.
paragraphs.simple: A tiger was lying on the ground, not moving. Its front foot was caught in a trap.

paragraphs.context: “No, he’s still breathing,” Annie said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tiger is very tired, not dead.
paragraphs.simple: The tiger is alive. He is very tired from trying to get free. The sad sound in the night was this tiger.

paragraphs.context: Poachers catch Indian tigers with steel traps.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why tigers are in danger.
paragraphs.simple: Poachers catch tigers in metal traps, which is not allowed. They kill the tigers and sell their bodies. If this does not stop, there may be no Indian tigers or rhinos left one day.
paragraphs.tone: Serious. This is a real problem in the world.

background.note: A steel trap is a metal trap with strong jaws. It shuts on an animal's leg when the animal steps on it.

paragraphs.context: “Okay,” he said. He showed the picture to Annie. “Here’s the plan.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack makes a plan to open the trap.
paragraphs.simple: Jack will push down on the trap to open it. Then Annie will pull the tiger's leg out.

paragraphs.context: He was the most majestic creature Jack had ever seen.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tiger is very beautiful.
paragraphs.simple: The tiger was the most wonderful animal Jack had ever seen, with a big orange head and black and white stripes.

paragraphs.context: Slowly, silently, Annie freed the tiger’s leg.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They free the tiger.
paragraphs.simple: Annie took the tiger's leg out of the trap and touched his fur gently. She told him to get better.
paragraphs.tone: "Slowly, silently" is used again and again, so we feel how careful and quiet they are.

paragraphs.context: The tiger was on his feet. He stared right at them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tiger is awake and comes toward them.
paragraphs.simple: The tiger was standing. He looked straight at them, made an angry sound and walked toward them.

paragraphs.context: But the tiger didn’t turn away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tiger still comes toward them.
paragraphs.simple: Jack made a noise, but the tiger did not stop. His eyes shone with anger and he showed his teeth.

paragraphs.context: She grabbed Jack’s hand and pulled him over to the bank.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They hide behind a rock.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pulled Jack to the side of the stream and they hid behind a rock. Jack is worried about Teddy.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard Teddy’s barks turn to fierce growls.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy fights the tiger.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy's small barks became big, angry growls, louder and louder. They did not sound like Teddy at all.

paragraphs.context: Teddy stood tall and brave in the grass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy has made the tiger go away.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy stood bravely. The tiger was walking away.

paragraphs.context: All the forest seemed to hold its breath
paragraphs.mainIdea: Everyone is happy that Teddy saved them.
paragraphs.simple: The forest was very quiet, as if it was waiting. Then Annie spoke: Teddy is a wonderful dog!

paragraphs.context: Arf! Arf! Teddy was just like a small scruffy dog again.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy is a little dog again.
paragraphs.simple: Now Teddy looked like a small, untidy dog again. He moved his tail and ran to them.

paragraphs.context: “How did you drive away that tiger?” asked Jack
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wonders how Teddy did it.
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks how Teddy made the tiger leave. Did he become a wild dog for a moment?
paragraphs.tone: A mystery: who is Teddy really?

paragraphs.context: “Well, I guess we won’t be getting a thank-you gift from that tiger,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: A joke from Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack jokes that the angry tiger will not give them a present to say thank you.

paragraphs.context: The water shimmered in the early light.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They follow the monkeys along the stream.
paragraphs.simple: The water shone in the morning light. Fish jumped. The animals went around a turn in the stream.

paragraphs.context: When they went around the bend, they saw a man sitting cross-legged on a rock.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They meet an old man.
paragraphs.simple: They saw a man with long white hair and a white beard, sitting on a rock with his eyes closed. He looked very calm.

paragraphs.context: Kah and Ko smoothed the man’s hair with their little paws
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkeys love the old man.
paragraphs.simple: The monkeys touched the man's hair and face gently. He smiled and talked softly to them.

paragraphs.context: “Knock, knock,” Annie said softly.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says hello in a funny way.
paragraphs.simple: There is no door, but Annie says "Knock, knock" to say she is there.

paragraphs.context: He turned his face toward Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The man cannot see.
paragraphs.simple: The man's eyes were open, but he did not see them. Jack understood that the man was blind.

paragraphs.context: “Hermits live far away from other people,” said the blind man.
paragraphs.mainIdea: What a hermit is.
paragraphs.simple: A hermit lives alone, away from people, to think. This man lives in the forest to learn from nature.

background.note: In India and many other places, some wise people live alone in forests or mountains. They think, pray and live a simple life.

paragraphs.context: “To the chatter of the monkeys, the rumble of the elephant, the roar of the tiger,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The man listens to the forest.
paragraphs.simple: He listens to all the animals. After a long time, they all sound like one big voice: the voice of the forest.

paragraphs.context: Jack wondered why the hermit was changing the subject.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The man asks for a flower.
paragraphs.simple: Jack did not understand why the man started to talk about a flower. Annie brought him a white flower with its muddy root.

paragraphs.context: “This perfect lotus blossom grows from dark, thick mud,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lesson of the lotus.
paragraphs.simple: The beautiful flower grows from dirty mud. You cannot have the beauty without the dirt.

background.note: The lotus is a water flower that grows out of mud but is very clean and beautiful. In India it is a sign of beauty and goodness.

paragraphs.context: “When you saved the tiger, you saved all of him,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lesson about the tiger.
paragraphs.simple: When they saved the tiger, they saved his beauty and also his wild, dangerous side. A tiger has both, like the lotus.
paragraphs.tone: This is the main lesson of the book.

paragraphs.context: “Take this lotus as a thank-you gift from all the forest
paragraphs.mainIdea: They get the third gift.
paragraphs.simple: The man gives them the lotus as a thank-you present from the forest. It is the "gift from a forest far away".

paragraphs.context: “Do not worry,” said the blind man. “Your house in the trees is close by.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is near.
paragraphs.simple: The elephants walked in a big circle all night, so they are back near the tree house.

paragraphs.context: The man held her hand for a moment.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels calm.
paragraphs.simple: The man held their hands. Jack suddenly felt very calm all over.

paragraphs.context: “You were great tour guides,” said Jack. “Good-bye.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They say goodbye to the monkeys.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thanks the monkeys for showing them around, like people who show visitors a place.

paragraphs.context: Inside the tree house, Jack picked up the Pennsylvania book.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They get ready to go home.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took the book about their home. But first he and Annie looked out of the window one more time.

background.note: The Pennsylvania book has a picture of the Frog Creek woods. The tree house uses it to take them home.

paragraphs.context: In the distance, they saw Saba and the other elephants bathing in the stream.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see all their animal friends again.
paragraphs.simple: From the tree house they saw the elephants washing, the monkeys swinging, the tiger lying in the sun and the old man smiling.
paragraphs.tone: Happy and peaceful: everyone is safe.

paragraphs.context: She put the lotus blossom beside the pocket watch from the Titanic
paragraphs.mainIdea: Now they have three gifts.
paragraphs.simple: Annie put the flower next to the other two gifts. One more gift and Teddy will be free.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, tell me this,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How did Annie know what Teddy wanted?
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks how Annie knew Teddy wanted them to hide. She says she saw it in his eyes.

paragraphs.context: Teddy’s eyes twinkled, as if they held many secrets.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy seems to have secrets.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy's eyes shone, as if he knew many things he could not tell. Jack asks him who he really is.
paragraphs.tone: A mystery for the next book.

paragraphs.context: The Frog Creek woods were very tame after the forest in India.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Home is quiet and safe.
paragraphs.simple: After the wild Indian forest, the Frog Creek woods felt very safe and quiet.

paragraphs.context: “I have two questions,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wonders how the blind man knew so much.
paragraphs.simple: How did the blind man know about the tree house, and about their night with the elephants? Annie says the voice of the forest told him.

paragraphs.context: All the sounds were like one great voice—the one great voice of home.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack listens to the sounds of home.
paragraphs.simple: Jack closes his eyes and listens, like the hermit. All the sounds of his street become one voice: the voice of home.

paragraphs.context: Adult elephants are plant eaters.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts about elephants.
paragraphs.simple: Grown-up elephants eat only plants. They eat for 15 hours a day, more than 180 kilos of plants.

background.note: 400 pounds is about 180 kilograms.

paragraphs.context: A giant python can grow up to 30 feet in length.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts about pythons.
paragraphs.simple: A very big python can be about 9 metres long.

paragraphs.context: India has 238 kinds of snakes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts about snakes in India.
paragraphs.simple: India has 238 kinds of snakes. The biggest is the python and one of the smallest is the worm snake, about 10 centimetres long.

paragraphs.context: Hinduism is the main religion of the people of India.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hanuman, a Hindu god.
paragraphs.simple: Most people in India follow Hinduism. This religion has many gods. One important god is Hanuman, who saved the goddess Sita.

paragraphs.context: Hanuman has the body of a man and the face
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why langurs are special.
paragraphs.simple: Hanuman looks like a man with the face and tail of a langur monkey. So Hindus treat langur monkeys as special guests at their temples.

paragraphs.context: In the nineteenth century, there were more than 40,000 tigers in India.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tigers are in danger.
paragraphs.simple: About 200 years ago, India had more than 40,000 tigers. Now it has fewer than 4,000, so tigers may soon die out.

paragraphs.context: The Wildlife Protection Society of India has been formed
paragraphs.mainIdea: A group that protects animals.
paragraphs.simple: This group helps save India's animals that are in danger. It catches people who hunt against the law and takes away things like tiger skins and ivory.

sentences.context: Years ago, I spent several months in India and found it to be a spectacularly colorful and interesting country.
sentences.simple: Many years ago I lived in India for some months. I thought it was a very colourful and interesting country.
sentences.main: I spent several months in India.

sentences.context: She and Jack looked around the tree house for one of the research books that Morgan always left them.

sentences.context: Using their long tails and arms, they swung from branch to branch.

parts.text: The langurs slowed down,
parts.meaning: The monkeys went slower,

parts.text: as if they understood Jack’s words.
parts.meaning: and it seemed that they understood what Jack said.

sentences.grammar: "As if" means "it seemed that". We do not know if it is really true.

sentences.context: And like many smaller cats, tigers often avoid wild dogs.
sentences.simple: Tigers often stay away from wild dogs, like many small cats do.
sentences.main: Tigers often avoid wild dogs.

parts.text: And like many smaller cats,
parts.meaning: And in the same way as many small cats,

parts.text: tigers often avoid wild dogs.
parts.meaning: tigers often stay away from wild dogs.

sentences.grammar: A tiger is a very big cat. "Like many smaller cats" compares it with small cats.

sentences.context: The bright orange had faded to a twilight gray.
sentences.simple: The bright orange sky slowly became evening grey.
sentences.main: The bright orange had faded.

parts.text: The bright orange had faded
parts.meaning: The bright orange colour had slowly gone

parts.text: to a twilight gray.
parts.meaning: and the sky was now the grey of early evening.

sentences.grammar: "Faded to ..." tells you what the colour changed into. "Had faded" happened before the moment in the story.

sentences.context: To kill its prey, the python squeezes it to death, then swallows it whole.
sentences.simple: A python kills an animal by holding it very tightly. Then it eats the animal in one piece.
sentences.main: The python squeezes it to death.

parts.text: To kill its prey,
parts.meaning: To kill the animal it hunts,

parts.text: the python squeezes it to death,
parts.meaning: the python presses it until it dies,

parts.text: then swallows it whole.
parts.meaning: then eats it all in one go, without chewing.

sentences.grammar: "To kill ..." at the start tells you why. "Then" shows the next step.

sentences.context: A python can swallow an animal the size of a full-grown deer.
sentences.simple: A python can eat an animal as big as an adult deer.
sentences.main: A python can swallow an animal.

parts.text: A python can swallow an animal
parts.meaning: A python is able to eat an animal

parts.text: the size of a full-grown deer.
parts.meaning: as big as an adult deer.

sentences.grammar: "The size of ..." means "as big as ...".

sentences.context: He let go of his vine and held on tightly to a branch.
sentences.simple: He stopped holding the vine and held a branch very tightly.
sentences.main: He let go and held on.

parts.text: He let go of his vine
parts.meaning: He stopped holding his long plant

parts.text: and held on tightly to a branch.
parts.meaning: and held a branch very strongly.

sentences.grammar: "Let go of" and "hold on to" are opposites: stop holding, keep holding.

sentences.context: When her feet rested on the elephant’s back, she let go of the branch.
sentences.simple: As soon as her feet were on the elephant's back, she stopped holding the branch.
sentences.main: She let go of the branch.

parts.text: When her feet rested on the elephant’s back,
parts.meaning: When her feet were on the elephant's back,

parts.text: she let go of the branch.
parts.meaning: she stopped holding the branch.

sentences.grammar: The "when" part tells you the time of the main action.

sentences.context: Kah and Ko bounded ahead of them, two moon shadows leading the way.
sentences.simple: Kah and Ko jumped along in front of them. In the moonlight they looked like two dark shapes showing the way.
sentences.main: Kah and Ko bounded ahead of them.

parts.text: Kah and Ko bounded ahead of them,
parts.meaning: Kah and Ko ran with big jumps in front of them,

parts.text: two moon shadows leading the way.
parts.meaning: like two dark shapes in the moonlight, showing where to go.

sentences.grammar: The part after the comma is a picture of Kah and Ko. "Moon shadows" are dark shapes made by moonlight.

sentences.context: It sounded as if the whole forest were moaning.
sentences.simple: It seemed that all the forest was making a long, sad sound.
sentences.main: It sounded as if the forest were moaning.

parts.text: It sounded
parts.meaning: It seemed, from the sound,

parts.text: as if the whole forest were moaning.
parts.meaning: that all the forest was crying in pain.

sentences.grammar: "Sounded as if" means "seemed, from what you hear". "Were" is used after "as if" for something not really true.

sentences.context: He began drifting in and out of dreams—dreams of rocking in a boat under the dark treetops.
sentences.simple: He started to sleep, wake a little and sleep again. He dreamed he was in a boat under dark trees.
sentences.main: He began drifting in and out of dreams.

parts.text: He began drifting in and out of dreams
parts.meaning: He started to fall asleep and wake up again and again

parts.text: —dreams of rocking in a boat under the dark treetops.
parts.meaning: —he dreamed of moving gently in a boat under dark trees.

sentences.grammar: The long dash adds more about the dreams. The elephant's walk feels like a boat.

sentences.context: But because they do not see well, they sometimes charge at things by mistake.
sentences.simple: Rhinos cannot see well, so sometimes they run at things when they do not mean to.
sentences.main: They sometimes charge at things.

parts.text: But because they do not see well,
parts.meaning: But since their eyes are not good,

parts.text: they sometimes charge at things by mistake.
parts.meaning: they sometimes run hard at things without meaning to.

sentences.grammar: "Because" gives the reason. "By mistake" = not on purpose.

sentences.context: People called poachers kill them and sell their body parts as medicine and good-luck charms.
sentences.simple: Bad people, called poachers, kill rhinos. They sell parts of their bodies as medicine and lucky things.
sentences.main: People kill them and sell their body parts.

parts.text: People called poachers
parts.meaning: Some people, who are called poachers,

parts.text: kill them
parts.meaning: kill the rhinos

parts.text: and sell their body parts
parts.meaning: and sell parts of their bodies

parts.text: as medicine and good-luck charms.
parts.meaning: for people to use as medicine or as things that bring luck.

sentences.grammar: "Called poachers" gives the name of these people. "As" here means "to be used as".

sentences.context: He must have gotten caught last night.
sentences.simple: I am sure he was caught in the trap last night.
sentences.main: He must have gotten caught.

parts.text: He must have gotten caught
parts.meaning: I am almost sure he was caught

parts.text: last night.
parts.meaning: last night.

sentences.grammar: "Must have + done" means you are almost sure something happened in the past.

sentences.context: Extinction means that someday there may be no Indian tigers or rhinos left on earth.
sentences.simple: "Extinction" means that one day all the Indian tigers and rhinos may be gone.
sentences.main: Extinction means that there may be no tigers left.

parts.text: Extinction means
parts.meaning: The word "extinction" means

parts.text: that someday there may be no Indian tigers or rhinos
parts.meaning: that one day there may not be any Indian tigers or rhinos

parts.text: left on earth.
parts.meaning: still living in the world.

sentences.grammar: "That ..." tells you what the word means. "Left" here means still there.

sentences.context: He was the most majestic creature Jack had ever seen.
sentences.simple: Jack had never seen an animal as great and beautiful as this tiger.
sentences.main: He was the most majestic creature.

parts.text: He was the most majestic creature
parts.meaning: The tiger was the greatest and most beautiful animal

parts.text: Jack had ever seen.
parts.meaning: of all the animals Jack had seen in his life.

sentences.grammar: "The most ... I had ever seen" means it was the best one of all.

sentences.context: All the forest seemed to hold its breath—until Annie broke the silence.
sentences.simple: The whole forest was very quiet and waiting, until Annie spoke.
sentences.main: All the forest seemed to hold its breath.

parts.text: All the forest seemed to hold its breath
parts.meaning: The whole forest was so quiet, as if it stopped breathing

parts.text: —until Annie broke the silence.
parts.meaning: —then Annie was the first to speak.

sentences.grammar: The forest does not really breathe. This is a picture: everything was still and quiet.

sentences.context: I have listened for so long, they have all begun to sound like one voice—the one great voice of the forest.
sentences.simple: I have listened to them for a very long time, and now they all sound like one voice: the voice of the forest.
sentences.main: They have all begun to sound like one voice.

parts.text: I have listened for so long,
parts.meaning: Because I have listened for a very long time,

parts.text: they have all begun to sound like one voice
parts.meaning: all the animals now seem to be one voice

parts.text: —the one great voice of the forest.
parts.meaning: —the big voice of the whole forest.

sentences.grammar: "Have listened" means from the past until now. The dash tells you more about "one voice".

sentences.context: Its beauty cannot live without its ugliness.
sentences.simple: The beautiful flower cannot grow without the dirty mud.
sentences.main: Its beauty cannot live without its ugliness.

parts.text: Its beauty cannot live
parts.meaning: The flower's beautiful part cannot be there

parts.text: without its ugliness.
parts.meaning: without its ugly, dirty part.

sentences.grammar: "Cannot ... without ..." means you need both. Beauty and ugliness are opposites.

sentences.context: You saved his graceful beauty—and his fierce, savage nature.
sentences.simple: You saved the beautiful tiger, and also the wild, dangerous tiger.
sentences.main: You saved his beauty and his nature.

parts.text: You saved his graceful beauty
parts.meaning: You saved his beautiful, smooth way of moving

parts.text: —and his fierce, savage nature.
parts.meaning: —and also his wild, dangerous side.

sentences.grammar: The dash makes you stop and think about part 2. "Nature" here means what the tiger is really like inside.

sentences.context: As they walked to their house, the last bit of daylight was slipping away.
sentences.simple: While they walked home, it was getting dark.
sentences.main: The last bit of daylight was slipping away.

parts.text: As they walked to their house,
parts.meaning: While they walked home,

parts.text: the last bit of daylight was slipping away.
parts.meaning: the last small part of the day's light was going.

sentences.grammar: "As" here means "while". "Slipping away" means going away slowly and quietly.

sentences.context: India has 238 kinds of snakes, ranging from the giant python to the worm snake, which is just over 4 inches long.
sentences.simple: There are 238 kinds of snakes in India. The biggest is the python and the smallest is the worm snake, about 10 centimetres long.
sentences.main: India has 238 kinds of snakes.

parts.text: India has 238 kinds of snakes,
parts.meaning: There are 238 kinds of snakes in India,

parts.text: ranging from the giant python to the worm snake,
parts.meaning: from the very big python to the worm snake,

parts.text: which is just over 4 inches long.
parts.meaning: which is only a little more than 10 centimetres long.

sentences.grammar: "Ranging from A to B" tells you the biggest and the smallest. "Which ..." tells you more about the worm snake.

all my best.meaning: A friendly way to end a letter, like "Best wishes".

all set.example: “All set?” Jack asked the little dog.

and all.meaning: "Root and all" means the root came up too, with the rest of the plant.

around a bend.meaning: Past the place where a river or road turns.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that something is true.
as if.example: as if laughing at Annie’s joke

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: they are about to set out

branch to branch.meaning: From one branch of a tree to another.
branch to branch.example: they swung from branch to branch

break the silence.meaning: To make the first sound after a time of quiet.

burst into laughter.meaning: To suddenly start to laugh loudly.

burst out laughing.meaning: To suddenly start to laugh loudly.

by mistake.meaning: Not on purpose; without wanting to.
by mistake.example: they sometimes charge at things by mistake

catch up.meaning: To come up to someone who is in front of you, by going faster.
catch up.example: Teddy waited for Jack and Annie to catch up.

change the subject.meaning: To start talking about something different.

chill down your spine.meaning: A sudden cold feeling down your back, because you are very afraid.
chill down your spine.example: A chill went down Jack’s spine.

close by.example: Your house in the trees is close by.

come in peace.meaning: "We come in peace" means "We are friends. We will not hurt you."

cross legged.meaning: Sitting on the floor with your knees out and your feet under your legs. (Usually written "cross-legged".)

drive away.meaning: To make someone or something go away.
drive away.example: How did you drive away that tiger?

feet first.meaning: With your feet going first, before the rest of your body.

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: I know how to find out

get going.meaning: To start to go; to leave now.

get well.meaning: To become healthy again after being sick or hurt.

go on.meaning: To continue; to keep talking or reading.

good luck.meaning: Something good that happens by chance. "Good-luck charms" are things people carry because they think they bring good luck.

got it.meaning: "Got it?" means "Do you understand?" "Got it" means "Yes, I understand."

hold on to.meaning: To hold something tightly so that you do not fall or lose it.
hold on to.example: held on tightly to a branch

hold out.meaning: To put your hand or arm out toward someone.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time. "The forest seemed to hold its breath" means everything was very quiet and waiting.
hold your breath.example: All the forest seemed to hold its breath

i bet.example: “I bet he is her brother,” said Annie.

i guess.meaning: "I guess" means "I think so, but I am not sure."

in a minute.example: A tiger would eat you in a minute.

in a panic.meaning: Very afraid, so that you cannot think clearly.

in and out of.meaning: "Drifting in and out of dreams" means falling asleep, then waking a little, then sleeping again.
in and out of.example: drifting in and out of dreams

in danger of.meaning: In a situation where something bad may happen.
in danger of.example: in danger of disappearing from the earth

in line.meaning: One behind the other, in a long line.
in line.example: The rest of the herd followed in line.

in search of.example: in search of the third gift

in shock.meaning: Very surprised and upset, so that you cannot think clearly.

knock knock.meaning: "Knock, knock" is what you say when you knock on a door (or pretend to), to ask if you can come in. It is also how a kind of joke starts.

lead the way.meaning: To go in front and show others where to go.
lead the way.example: two moon shadows leading the way

let go of.example: He let go of his vine

let out.example: The elephant let out a low rumbling sound

let someone out.meaning: To let a person or animal come out of a place, like a bag, box or room.
let someone out.example: Jack let Teddy out of his pack.

life or death.meaning: Very, very serious, because someone may die.

lost at sea.meaning: A ship "lost at sea" sank in the sea and was never found again.
lost at sea.example: A gift from a ship lost at sea,

make sure.meaning: To check that something is true or will happen.
make sure.example: as if to make sure he was okay

no longer.example: The sky above was no longer glowing.

not so fast.meaning: "Not so fast" means "Wait, don't be happy too soon." There is more to hear.

of course.meaning: Yes, surely. You say it when the answer is clear.

on his feet.example: The tiger was on his feet.

pay attention.meaning: To watch, listen to or think about something carefully. "Paid no attention" means did not listen or care.

push off.meaning: To push hard against something with your feet or hands to start moving.

run and hide.meaning: To run away to a place where no one can see you.

run into.meaning: To meet someone when you did not plan to.

set out.example: Now they are about to set out in search of the third gift

slip away.meaning: To go away slowly and quietly. "The daylight was slipping away" means it was getting dark.
slip away.example: the last bit of daylight was slipping away

soaking wet.example: She was barefoot and soaking wet.

squeeze your eyes shut.meaning: To close your eyes very tightly.

stand on end.meaning: When your hair stands on end, it stands up straight because you are very afraid.

take off.meaning: To leave or run away suddenly and fast.
take off.example: took off for the magic tree house

take out.meaning: To take something out of a bag or pocket.
take out.example: Jack started to take out his notebook.

thank you gift.meaning: A present that you give to say thank you. (Usually written "thank-you gift".)

time for dinner.meaning: "Time for dinner" means "Dinner is ready. Come and eat."

too bad.meaning: "Too bad" means "It is a pity" or "That is sad."
too bad.example: Too bad animals can’t wear glasses

touch your heart.meaning: To make you feel sad, kind or full of love.

turn away.meaning: To turn your body or face so that you look in another direction.

turn into.meaning: To change and become something different.

under a spell.meaning: Controlled by magic, so that you cannot be or do what you usually are or do.
under a spell.example: This little dog is under a spell

up and down.meaning: Going up and then down, again and again.

visit with.meaning: To spend time talking with someone. (American English.)
visit with.example: Would you like to visit with me?

wash over.meaning: When a feeling washes over you, you suddenly feel it in all your body, like a wave.
wash over.example: Jack felt a wave of calm wash over him.

with a start.meaning: Suddenly, with a small jump, because you are surprised.
with a start.example: He opened his eyes with a start.

oh man.meaning: Something you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. "Oh, man!" is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a real man.

oh brother.meaning: "Oh, brother!" is something you say when you feel a little tired of something or think it is silly. Annie makes a joke about it, because Ko really is Kah's brother.

yeah right.meaning: "Yeah, right" here means "I don't believe you!" Jack says the opposite of what he thinks.
